Answering as an acoustician.

I’ve been writing popular science for almost a year now. I can’t change the fact that acoustics is a niche field, but I have found an audience. At least some people have gotten something out of my articles and learned about acoustics, and through outreach I’ve met some excellent colleagues. I’ve learned a lot and enjoyed it, and that’s what has kept me going.

Here are some lessons from the writing process that I’d like to share. Some of the images come from my talk at China’s National Acoustics Conference in September.

First, why I started writing popular science on Zhihu and a WeChat Official Account. There were roughly three reasons:

  • Recognition
  • Sharing knowledge
  • Leaving a mark

The first two are easy to understand. When I first heard the last one, I didn’t believe it either, but it really is one of my motives. A hundred years from now, 99.99% of the people on Earth today will be gone, but writing and knowledge last forever, so I want to leave my mark on the world. Yep, it’s that corny.

Whatever the reason, motivation is the first step in anything, and popular science is no exception.

That’s the first step. Now for some concrete lessons from my own experience.

  1. Passion. Once you have a basic motive, loving what you do gives you an endless supply of energy.
  2. Understand your material completely. Actually, that doesn’t quite capture it. To explain a concept well enough for a general audience takes at least twice as long as simply learning it; understanding alone isn’t enough. Popular science is different from academic writing, which throws formulas at you and explains principles, objective, rational and logically watertight, mostly for people who already understand. Popular science is written precisely for people who mostly don’t, and getting the message across takes more skill. Sometimes I even think popular science is harder than writing papers.
  3. Plain language. Picture first ↓. Many of you have probably seen the conversation between Alibaba founder Jack Ma and Tesla’s Elon Musk at a summit a while back; the picture below sums it up. Jack Ma comes from business and probably doesn’t even know these technical terms in Chinese. Plain language matters more than anything in popular science: it has to be approachable, conversational and down to earth, or your readers will be as lost as Jack Ma.

4. Don’t be stiff: fewer formulas, more pictures and examples. I like to use all kinds of images, the cooler and more mind-blowing the better. High-resolution images also make an article more pleasant to read and put readers in a good mood. Take the cover image of this article:

A history of acoustics: auralization

5. Engage more than one sense, with video and audio, for example. I’ve always felt that information taken in by the eyes alone is monotonous. As someone who works in acoustics, I have to make some noise, so that reading isn’t monotonous and readers remember it. For example, in the answer below I included a video to explain how we perceive space.

How do we perceive how high or low a sound is?

This article is fairly heavy going, so I used lots of animations:

Particle velocity: sound is about more than pressure

And this article has several videos:

A history of acoustics: architectural acoustics


6. Humor. As a Northeasterner, I have joking around in my blood. Growing up on the black soil of Northeast China filled me to the brim with errenzhuan (the region’s rowdy song-and-comedy duets), I mean, with artistic talent. See the picture below.

7. Strong logic. Before you type the first word, sort out the logic of the whole piece, and only start writing once you’ve thought it through yourself. If you think as you write and don’t even know where the logic is yourself, don’t expect readers to follow it.

8. Write often, to build up your writing skills.


One picture to sum it all up

I’ve been quiet lately. Partly I’ve been busy; partly I’ve been thinking about where to take my Zhihu and WeChat accounts. I’m delighted that another writer, with many years of clinical experience in acoustics, has joined my team to run the outreach with me. We certainly won’t be the fastest to post, one article every two weeks, but we can guarantee quality: every article is discussed and polished by both of us. I hope more people will see them and get to know acoustics.
